articles.title: Carnegie Mellon is putting computer science courses on YouTube for free
articles.summary: Carnegie Mellon is putting computer science courses on YouTube for free

top_comments: Hi! I'm Phillip Compeau, I teach in Carnegie Mellon's Griffin School of Computer Science, and I run CS Learn, which launched today.We're releasing full semesters of lectures from current CMU computer science courses across a variety of topics, with one course premiering each day this week. More courses come in January.Yes, MIT got here 25 years ago :). What I'm excited about is how we're doing it: a few of our students built tools that automate a lot of the production work, so a small team can get a course out quickly and still have people review every lecture.We'll have lots more coming across a wide array of subjects. I'd love to know if there are topics you would like to see us cover!

top_comments: Just as AI has advanced massively in the past two years, I think a lot of gamers would be shocked at how viable Linux is as a genuine gaming platform in 2026. I already have plans to switch from Windows to Linux, I even have Linux running from an external drive to play with it.The vast vast majority of single player games are 100% perfect on Linux. Multiplayer still has lots of hiccups.

I've been a heavy macOS user for dev work since early adolescence. Before that I used FreeBSD, so I'm comfortable with the command line. (Yes, you read that right.) But it's been a while since I used anything other than macOS for serious development work. A lot of the shenanigans around macOS Tahoe made me seriously consider switching to Linux. Last month I finally got the gumption and set up a Linux desktop how I like it.I see no reason why any developer, other than someone writing something for the Windows platform specifically, should not be using Linux over Windows. MacOS has a ton of polish in so many places—but then there are all these little paper cuts that keep coming: funny little bugs that interrupt work or make you scratch your head. Peeking over the garden wall into Windows' garden only seems worse. Linux by comparison is awesome! I look forward to spending my day on my Linux desktop.Seriously, if you do dev work, do yourself a favor and boot up—I dunno, maybe Fedora Silverblue—on a separate partition and force yourself to work on it for a day or two. Use an LLM to diagnose issues as they come up. (I had some serious stability issues; Claude suggested it was a memory issue; running memtest86 told me I had bad RAM—fixing that and all problems went away.) You'll find that your system is quieter and less distracting.I still don't think Linux is for "average users"—even though most people probably only need a web browser. But if you have gone anywhere near a command line in your life, it will be worth the switch.

For anyone on the fence about switching from Windows to Linux: it takes about a week, if that, of adjusting. If most of what you do is on the Web already (and the services you use provide a Web-based client), you have nothing to lose but your chains.Take your pick - Ubuntu, Fedora, someone else mentioned Mint. All fine choices, no wrong answers.

articles.summary: Jiff 1.0: A datetime library for Rust

top_comments: I maintained chrono for about half a decade, and the specific reason I took on maintenance was because the API sucked and I hoped I could make it better.Turns out, the reason people wanted to use it was because the API was stable and every slight step towards improvement was met with... resistance. I stopped maintaining it because the burnout from seeing what it could be and not seeing any path to get there was too much for me.I'm extremely grateful to burntsushi for writing the datetime library rust deserves. Chrono is stable and is maintained (though semi-deprecated) by an extremely reliable rustacean -- you don't need to leave, but you'll probably be happier if you do.

> When should I use Jiff? Jiff isn’t always the right thing to use.I really appreciate when a project calmly acknowledges that it's not the right tool for every use case, and is not trying to be. top_comments: The whole concept of Google Tag Manager was that you could give marketing departments the ability to add "tags" to the website without having to involve engineering. That's how we got 10MB of javascript with every news article.I hope folks are re-evaluating that now.

This stuff is so avoidable but unless we implement meaningful reprocussions things aren't going to change. There is no accountability.In this case optimizely should have had better systems to spot a release like this (internal cool downs, check and balances, phased rolouts, automatic security checks). And sites that have massive user bases (cnn, bbc, etc..) have zero excuse to not have the same.I would go so far as to say those sites should not be serving from vendors but should be vendoring their own scripts that they also are passing through security audits and serving them selves with cool downs.How do these companies not have better dedication to protecting their users is beyond me.
Subresource Integrity has been available for over a decade. It’s time to start implementing it with these services.

articles.title: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays
articles.summary: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays

top_comments: There's a stretch in California Interstate 5 near the town of Coalinga where you will see acres and acres of cows baking under the naked sun in the summertime and they huddle next to each other to find a brief relief of nonexistent protection from the searing sun. You just wonder why their owners cannot come up with a single idea on how to give them shade. It's cruelty.

There are lots of use cases for solar with livestock and livestock + agriculture.China has fish farms with solar, reflection from water increases efficiency by 5%: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MgQVV0_75j0Livestock need shade, and grass doesn't need continuous shade grows better in shade in most tropical climates. If its too hot, grass dies off. Livestock also need ACs when temperatures reach 50+ centigrade, which can be powered by solar.Cows are ruminants, they lie down and ruminate for hours in shade.Except for goats, solar works with most animals.Solar can always be used as a fence (zero land use, zero interruption to machinery) and get paid at a higher rate in the mornings and evenings, extending solar production window by ~4 hours.Farming is tough and low status. All countries support farming with subsidies. The best use of farms is solar+ anything else. Photosynthesis is 6% efficiency (and it goes down to less than 1% when we use it for livestock feed or ethanol with conversion losses), solar is ~25%. Solar has zero opex and can run for 3 - 5 decades, output can be used directly.

The introduction of solar is something that my rural Appalachian county has dealt with recently.There was considerable pushback from the 60+ crowd and NIMBY types just like there is for everything new and different, but we got three permitted and are waiting on them to begin construction.The thing that got me was there was a lot of people that just made whatever argument they could to try and stop it. All kinds of arguments that people either didn't understand or didn't really believe in. They just knew they hated solar. I really couldn't wrap my head around it.From my perspective. It's a net good for our ranchers. We're mostly small family ranches, 200 head or less and the lease paid by the solar company helps these folks meet the bottom line. Beef prices won't stay up forever so it's a good time to diversify.
